metadata.reading_assignment: Sykes and Vanatko, Virtual Currencies and Money Laundering: Legal Background, Enforcement Actions, and Legislative Proposals

questions.question_stem: An explorer tags the 2-million-address cluster at the end of your trace "Exchange X" but shows no basis for the tag. What confidence does the course scale give the attribution?
questions.correct_answer: Low, because it rests on one label with no basis you can check.
incorrect_answers: Moderate, because a well-known explorer's tag is one strong line.
Moderate, because cluster size and a tag are two lines that agree.
High, because a cluster this large is nearly always a named service.
questions.explanation: A tag with no basis shown is one unverified label, and a cluster's size is behavior alone. Neither is a strong line, and they are not independent, so the attribution stays Low until a label of another kind agrees.

questions.question_stem: Exchange X publishes a list of its own wallet addresses, and the last address of your trace is on it. What does the list support, and what does it not?
questions.correct_answer: It is strong for the addresses it lists, because the owner holds the keys, but it says nothing about the addresses it leaves out.
incorrect_answers: It is strong for the whole cluster behind the address, because an owner would list every single address that it controls.
It is weak, because an owner has every reason to publish a list that flatters its own compliance record and hides the rest.
It is current for any date, because a published list never changes once the owner has posted it for the public to read.
questions.explanation: The owner knows its own keys, so a listed address is a strong label. The same list is silent on deposit addresses or wallets it did not publish, and lists change, so the exact address and the date matter.

questions.question_stem: A forum alias and an IP address analysis point to a named person as the operator of a mixing service. How far does this evidence carry on its own?
questions.correct_answer: It is a lead to a person or service that needs another line of evidence before anyone relies on it.
incorrect_answers: It is strong evidence of the operator, because forum posts and IP addresses are public and checkable.
It is as strong as a court record, because investigators gathered it in the course of a criminal case.
It is worthless, because off-chain information can never be tied to on-chain activity at all.
questions.explanation: Open-source intelligence is a lead. It points at a person or a service but needs a second line of a different kind, such as the cluster or a record, to carry weight.

questions.question_stem: A platform reports a cluster of about 900,000 addresses for a mixer. Investigators' own test deposits to the mixer landed in four of the five addresses they tested. How should you read the cluster?
questions.correct_answer: As a floor: the cluster likely leaves out some of the service's addresses, so the real count is higher.
incorrect_answers: As complete: four of five is close enough, so the cluster lists every address the mixer used in total.
As unreliable: one missed address means the whole cluster should be dropped from the assessment entirely.
As a ceiling: the platform merges owners freely, so the real count is lower than 900,000 addresses.
questions.explanation: A conservative platform leaves out addresses that belong to the service (underinclusion). The missed deposit shows that here, so the count is a floor. Merging unrelated owners is the opposite error and shows up in a different test.

questions.question_stem: An analyst merges two clusters whenever an output looks like change, without testing the guess. What is the risk?
questions.correct_answer: One wrong link joins everything behind it, so unrelated owners collapse into a single supercluster.
incorrect_answers: The clusters stay too small, because change guesses only ever leave out addresses that really belong.
The labels disappear, because merged clusters lose the tags that were attached to each part.
The analysis slows, because a larger cluster takes much longer to search than two small ones.
questions.explanation: Careless change merging builds clusters that hold many owners; one false link carries every address attached to it. This is over-merging, the opposite of the underinclusion a conservative platform shows.

questions.question_stem: A colleague writes "99.9% confident" next to a cluster label, citing a study that found a very low false-positive rate for the clustering method. What is wrong with the claim?
questions.correct_answer: The rate describes the method on the study's data, not this link, so give a word and the reason.
incorrect_answers: The rate is too low to trust, because a study this small cannot support so many nines in a report.
The rate is fine if two platforms agree, because agreement turns a method's rate into a link's rate.
The rate is right, but the wording is off: analysts should say 100% when a study found none.
questions.explanation: A study tests clustering against known answers and shows it works for most users and fails in known ways. Its error rate is for the method on that test set. The course gives each link Low, Moderate or High, never a percentage.

questions.question_stem: In the model explanation of Bitcoin Fog, suppose the investigators' own test deposits had never been made. Which part would change, and how?
questions.correct_answer: Part 4 falls from High to Moderate, because only clustering evidence of one kind would remain.
incorrect_answers: Part 2 changes most, because the number of addresses would drop below 900,000 without deposits.
Part 3 is dropped, because without deposits nothing about the group would be inferred at all.
Part 5 changes most, because the operator's identity would no longer come from records off the chain.
questions.explanation: The confidence in part 4 rests on two kinds of evidence agreeing: the clustering and deposits made to the service itself. Other tools that check the cluster are the same kind as the clustering, so without the deposits the word falls to Moderate.

questions.question_stem: The court accepted Chainalysis Reactor's clustering in the Bitcoin Fog case although the platform had no peer review and no known error rate. Which check was evidence of a different kind from the clustering?
questions.correct_answer: Investigators' own deposits to the service, four of five of which landed in the cluster.
incorrect_answers: A second platform agreeing on all 144 addresses that paid the defendant, as it did.
The defense's own tool confirming almost 400,000 addresses with no false positive found at all.
Both experts agreeing that the platform's clustering was conservative here on purpose.
questions.explanation: Deposits made to the service itself test the cluster against the service's behavior. A second platform and the defense's tool also cluster the chain, so they support the result but are the same kind of evidence.

questions.question_stem: Your trace reaches a cluster of over 900,000 addresses that you can name as a mixer. An agent asks who ran it. What do you say?
questions.correct_answer: The chain shows and sizes the service; who ran it comes from records off the chain, outside your own assessment.
incorrect_answers: The largest address in the cluster belongs to the operator, because the owner usually sits at its center.
The earliest address in the cluster names the operator, because the person funded the service at its launch.
High confidence on the cluster covers its operator too, because a service and its owner are one finding.
questions.explanation: In Bitcoin Fog, Samourai Wallet and Hydra, the chain found and sized the service. The people, their intent and control came from aliases, IP addresses, forum posts, servers and a government listing. The analyst's assessment stops at what the chain shows.

questions.question_stem: TRM and Chainalysis both tag the last cluster of your trace "Exchange X". Then Exchange X's own published list is found to include the final address. How does your confidence move?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate with two platforms agreeing, then High once the owner's list adds another kind.
incorrect_answers: High with two platforms agreeing, then no higher once the owner's own list is also added.
Moderate with two platforms agreeing, then still Moderate once the owner's list is added in.
Low with two platforms agreeing, then only Moderate once the owner's list is added to them.
questions.explanation: Two platforms run similar clustering heuristics over the same transactions, which is one kind of evidence. The owner's list is a label of another kind, so a cluster and a label that agree, with no known failure, reach High.

questions.question_stem: Under FinCEN's 2013 guidance, which actor is most likely to be treated as a money services business rather than an ordinary user?
questions.correct_answer: A business that accepts, transmits, buys, or sells convertible virtual currency for customers.
incorrect_answers: A person who buys virtual currency for personal purchases and uses it to pay merchants directly.
A noncustodial wallet developer who publishes code but does not control customer assets or transfers.
A merchant who accepts virtual currency for retail sales and later converts receipts at an exchange.
questions.explanation: The CRS reading emphasizes FinCEN's functional distinction: ordinary users are generally not MSBs, while administrators and exchangers operating as businesses may be money transmitters.

specific_source.anchor: FinCEN Guidance; User, administrator, exchanger distinction

questions.question_stem: AML compliance can be understood as an institutional data-production system. Which scenario best illustrates that mechanism?
questions.correct_answer: An exchange maintains customer records, monitors suspicious behavior, and files reports that investigators can later use with transaction traces.
incorrect_answers: A blockchain analytics company publishes address risk scores, but no covered institution collects customer records or files reports.
A decentralized protocol lets users swap assets through smart contracts, so compliance data depends mainly on public transaction events.
A court treats virtual currency as funds in a criminal case, but the case does not involve institutional monitoring or reporting duties.
questions.explanation: The CRS report explains that covered institutions have AML programs, recordkeeping, and suspicious activity reporting duties. Those duties create off-chain evidence that can connect to pseudonymous flows.

questions.question_stem: Which policy argument best reflects the legal uncertainty around virtual currency regulation?
questions.correct_answer: Clearer AML coverage can help enforcement, but broad or unclear duties may burden legitimate developers and noncustodial actors who do not control customer funds.
incorrect_answers: AML duties should attach to wallet software, validators, and noncustodial developers because uncertainty mostly protects criminals from court jurisdiction in practice.
Virtual currencies fall outside existing AML law unless Congress creates a crypto-specific statute, so agencies should delay enforcement against exchangers and processors.
Safe harbors should exempt custodial exchanges from suspicious-report and registration duties because innovation concerns outweigh customer records.
questions.explanation: The CRS reading presents a tradeoff: regulators and prosecutors need workable legal categories, while overly broad obligations can chill innovation or sweep in actors without customer custody or control.
